items.title: What 'augmentation, not replacement' means for a surgery
items.body: McCrory's finding — that AI so far complements expertise rather than replacing it, and that people with more domain knowledge get more out of it — maps neatly onto what an AI scribe actually does in a consulting room. The tool drafts the letter or the notes; the clinician still steers, corrects and signs. If McCrory is right, the sensible posture is to use these tools to widen what a GP can get through in a session while keeping the doctor firmly in the loop. If Zitron is right that the underlying economics are hollow, the practical caution is the same one that always applies to a cheap, venture-subsidised tool: do not build your workflow so tightly around it that you are stranded if the price jumps or the supplier folds.

items.title: Junior roles and training are the place to watch
items.body: The one soft signal in the essay is weaker hiring for young workers in AI-exposed roles — though McCrory rightly blames a low-hire, low-fire macro market as much as AI. For general practice and the wider NHS the read-across is about training pipelines rather than redundancy: if AI quietly absorbs the routine tasks that junior staff once cut their teeth on, someone has to make sure trainees, HCAs and new GPs still get the reps that build judgement. The augmentation story is only good news if the ladder underneath it is protected.

items.title: A money story with a clinical tail
items.body: Most of this edition is macroeconomics, not medicine, and it is fair to say the direct clinical content is thin. The honest takeaway for a practice is disposition, not diagnosis: whether or not you believe the productivity numbers, keep AI as an assistant with a clinician accountable for every output, and avoid long or expensive lock-ins premised on today's generous pricing being permanent.
